catalog_quote: Content words contain at least two vowels. Some functors, such as the conjunction ma ‘and’, are monosyllabic. Stress falls on the penultimate vowel of a word with secondary stress assigned to every second syllable to the left. All vowel sequences occur with the exception of /uo/. This includes double vowels (sequences of two identical vowels) /ii/, /ee/, /aa/, /oo/ and /uu/. Such double vowels are realised phonetically as a single long vowel, i.e. [iː], [ɛː], [aː], [ɔː] and [uː]. Given the placement of stress, one member of a vowel sequence will always bear stress. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate vowel of the word; secondary stress on every second vowel to the left of it (alternating trochaic pattern from the right). Since double vowels (VV) are phonetically long and one member of any vowel sequence is always stressed, a word-final double vowel surfaces as final stress on a long vowel (cf. Jonker 1915: 5-6, final accent on derivatives of monosyllabic roots).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated: 'secondary stress assigned to every second syllable to the left' (same wording for Termanu on p. 12).
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic functors (e.g. ma 'and') fall outside the disyllabic minimum; the nominal enclitic =a (Landu entry, p. 88) does not attract stress: 'Stress remains on the penultimate syllable of the host', the enclitic often being non-syllabic in citation form. Jonker 1915: 5-6 (Termanu) adds final accent on derivatives/compounds whose last member is a monosyllabic (long-vowel) root.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement made for the Rote languages as a group (sec. 2.4.1 covers all Rote lects, Rikou included) in a comparative dictionary's phonological overview, not a Rikou-specific description. Edwards has his own Rikou field data (Nov 2017; Table 1.2) and in Edwards 2018: 365-366 transcribes Rikou uraʔ [ˈʔʊraʔ], ʔuse-ʔ [ˈʔʊsɛʔ], au ʔuseʔ [ˌʔawˈʔʊsɛʔ] with penultimate primary and alternating secondary stress, consistent with the rule.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is made for the Rote languages collectively (Edwards 2021 sec. 2.4.1), which include Rikou/Ringgou with its dialects Landu and Oepao (= ring1244 [rgu]; Edwards's Table 2.2 lists Rikou proper as nucl1538, Landu as land1257, Oepao as oepa1237). It is not a Ringgou-specific phonological description; Edwards's Rikou field data and his stress-marked Rikou transcriptions (Edwards 2018: 365-366) are the Rikou-specific support. Jonker 1915's parallel rule is Termanu (term1237/pada1259)-based.

new_statements.quote: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root. The first vowel of vowel sequences carries the stress. Stress shifts to the right with the addition of syllabic object enclitics. In compounding of nouns and verbs, and in reduplication, it is the penultimate syllable of the final lexical root that bears primary word stress [' = secondary stress]. (1) ['rafu] 'ashes', ['lima-k] 'hand/arm' (2) ['oe] 'water', ['hai] 'stop, come to an end', ['tau-k] 'man' (3) ['tutu] 'pound', [tu'tuu-k] 'seat' ... (4) ['ina(-k)] 'mother', ['ina-g] 'my mother', [,ina-g-'ala] 'my mothers' (5) [,tasi 'oe] 'sea-water'

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (penultimate; Edwards 2021: 35) and adds the domain (the root), the vowel-sequence rule, compound/reduplication behaviour and secondary-stress marks. One detail differs from the other sources held by the project: Fox & Grimes say stress shifts right under syllabic object enclitics, whereas Edwards 2021: 88 (Landu article =a: 'Stress remains on the penultimate syllable of the host') and Jonker 1915: 5-6 (no shift under pronominal enclitics) say it does not. The sketch describes Rotinese as one language on the Termanu/Ba'a-based tradition (p. 613: 'Most of the early studies of Rotinese were in the dialects of Termanu and Ba'a'); Ringgou is named only as one of th…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the root; in a vowel sequence the first vowel is stressed (so ['oe], ['hai], ['tau-k] count the sequence as two syllables); syllabic object enclitics shift stress rightward; in compounds and reduplications the final lexical root carries primary stress (['tutu] 'pound' vs [tu'tuu-k] 'seat'); the -k/-g nominal suffixes do not attract stress (['lima-k], ['ina-g]).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated as a rule; the bracket '[, = secondary stress]' (scanned shows it as an apostrophe) and examples [,ina-g-'ala] 'my mothers' and [,tasi 'oe] 'sea-water' show a secondary stress on the non-final root of a suffixed or compound word.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shift to the right with syllabic object enclitics; compounds/reduplications stressed on the last root; first vowel of a vowel sequence stressed. p. 614 also: 'High and mid vowels have lax allophones in unstressed closed syllables.'
new_statements.identity_note: Fox & Grimes 1995 describe 'Roti' as one language on the Termanu/Ba'a-based descriptive tradition (p. 613), naming Ringgou only as an eastern dialect and for /nd/ > [r]; the stress section is not Ringgou-specific. Manafe 1889 writes from Baa (Ba'a) and groups Upao (Oepao), Ringgou and Landu together as one dialect ('lagu' 1, pp. 636-637). The PARADISEC OE9 collection (Bilbaa, Landu, Oepao, Rikou field notes) could not be opened. The catalog's penultimate rule for ring1244 still rests on the group-level statement in Edwards 2021: 35, whose Rote data include the author's own Rikou notes.

readall_conflicts: No source disagrees on the primary placement: Fox & Grimes 1995: 614 (penultimate syllable of the root, Rotinese generally) agrees with Edwards 2021: 35 (penultimate, Rote languages, with Rikou data) and Jonker 1915: 5-6 (Termanu). Two smaller points differ. (a) Enclitics: Fox & Grimes say 'Stress shifts to the right with the addition of syllabic object enclitics', whereas Edwards 2021: 88 (Landu =a: 'Stress remains on the penultimate syllable of the host') and Jonker 1915 (no stress shift under pronominal enclitics) say stress stays on the host; this may be a difference between object enclitics and the nominal article, or between dialects, and cannot be settled from these texts. (b) Manafe 1889: 634 says the reader's voice 'must fall on' the syllable closed by q, giving kuluq with the voice on the final luq; read as stress this would be a final-stressed form, but the sentence is more plausibly about where the glottal cut-off sits and is not a stress rule. Nothing opened contradicts penultimate stress for Rikou/Landu/Oepao specifically; no Ringgou-specific phonological statement exists in any opened work.
